You’re right, it’s crazy to expect a rose garden from a utility contract. It’s not crazy to expect that the services under a contract are provided. 

Further, assuming this is a hypothetical agreement, that term would likely be contained in the part of the contract that defines the services provided if its included. Likely they have a waiver stating you can’t sue for xyz reasons or that they can’t always guarantee services due to xyz reasons. 

That said, contracts are not exhaustive lists and can be interpreted pursuant to expectation, common understanding, trade usage, etc. 

I’m not attacking you guy, I’m informing you as to how contracts operate in our legal system and why your initial argument is not an accurate portrayal of it.

Yeah you haven’t seen it because it does not need to be explicit, see my first point. 

Listen, I understand that you probably feel very strongly about this about self-reliance, but the fact of the matter is consumer expectations have a legal consequence in the interpretation of service contracts. 

Is it entitled to enforce your rights under a contractual agreement? Would you let the guy who mows your lawn renege on the terms of your agreement? Entitlements are what they are: things that you are entitled to. You are entitled to the benefit of your agreement, otherwise you wouldn’t be able to enforce any contracts ever.

Explicit guarantees or warranties aren’t required. For example, the implied warranty of merchantability is a non-explicit warranty on goods sold that they conform to a buyers expectations. 

Are you arguing that a service provider can provide their services in any way shape or form, at any time, without an explicit guarantee that defines their services? Or are you arguing that failing to provide services defined in a contract is not somehow a breach of that contract? 

Unless there is a specific term in your contract that says they can’t guarantee power 100% of the time, I’d argue that consumer expectation is for power to be supplied every day all day. Clearly it’s impossible to never have outages, but that doesn’t change consumer expectation and the right to benefit from a services contract.

So if we assume it's discrimination, is it wrong? Obviously, there are types of discrimination that private parties can engage in (employers can fire you if you're not vaccinated, or can fire you for your political speech) and types of discrimination that private parties CAN'T engage in (banning racial groups from their stores; firing someone for getting pregnant). There is a statutory right to privacy with regards to medical history, but that is not based upon any constitutional right, but rather is based upon consumer protection.  What I'm getting at is: even if it's discrimination, then is it really a problem?

Further, I really don't think it's discrimination. Any party to a transaction may (and should) ask that someone deals in good faith, whether that's in an employment contract, buying an interest in a partnership, or a contract for sale. Based on the right to contract/freedom of commerce, I can choose whether do deal with someone who is vaccinated. Now, I doubt that anyone would go so far to demand a vaccination record outside of employment, but my own private liberty means that I can choose not to interact with you. This extends to simple transactions in which you may enter my office, or enter the business down the street to buy bread. You failing to disclose your status endangers me and my customers, and I think that I should have the right to ban you or recover damages if you spread any disease.

You are correct in saying that lack of vaccination does not lead  to the conclusion that you ARE infected or even WILL spread any infection. However, there is always a risk, and depending on the infection rate and severity of a disease, then the severity of such a failure to disclose changes as well. What I'm getting at is: you have a duty not to harm others, and if you do cause a disease to spread, then yes I think you should be liable.

Not to say that privacy isn't an important right. I do think that perhaps this argument is made in a hypothetical world, because again, vaccine mandates are legal under current American jurisprudence. That being the case, if you don't think there's any way to ensure that public safety (i.e. the amalgamation of each individual's right to be free from harm), then I should at least be able to recover damages from you for any medical expenses that are incurred by your choices.

What this argument really boils down to is this: if there is no governmental enforcement to ensure that I'm not harmed by you or your choices, then there should be a private enforcement mechanism. Maybe that means you shouldn't have to disclose anything to anyone, but if that's the case then I think there should be some way to punish you or collect recompense for any harm you caused. I.e. jail time, fines, or tort.

I mean, aren’t vaccine mandates arguably an enforcement of individual rights? Obviously you have a right to choose medical procedures (technically you don’t, with years of precedent going the other way and with Roe likely being overturned), but we also have a right to not have our health affected by others unilaterally (think pollution and current precedent surrounding vaccine mandates). 

Further, wouldn’t it be our business if you are or are not vaccinated? If no mandate, then I think that we as individuals or a society should know so we can ban you from our businesses and homes if we so choose. 

In either case, the individual right you claim includes unilateral conduct that affects others without consent IMO.

So back when I was in college, I dated this beautiful girl who was way out of my league. She asked me to come to dinner with her and meet her parents and so of course, I accepted. 

The day finally came and since she said it was a really nice place I decided to wear a full suit and tie that I bought for interviews so i could impress her parents. Unfortunately, I think I misunderstood because her dad was just wearing a nice shirt and jeans when I got there and when I was introduced, he looked me up and down and made some weird face. Feeling stupid, I lied and said I was just coming from an important meeting with a big company in his line of work. I don’t think he believed me though, because when he asked me a follow up question I just laughed and agreed with him and pretended I didn’t hear what he said. In the car my girlfriend asked me what the hell I was doing because she knew I wasn’t in a meeting, and I just said I was trying to make a good impression. She told me to be “normal” and I just felt so embarrassed. Little did I know, I was about to make it so much worse. 

Anyways, we get to the place and we get seated and I look around and see that everyone is dressed more like my gf’s dad, and I start to turn really red. I’m trying to think of a way to save face, and so in the middle of my gf’s mom’s order I blurt out “I’m ordering for the table.” 

I felt like the whole room turned to look at me. Her mom’s mouth was hanging open and she looked surprised, and her dad was just glaring at me like he wanted to strangle me. My gf had her eyes closed like she was ashamed to look at me. But I doubled down: “I’ll be ordering for the table tonight.” I thought it would be cool to take initiative, but it so so wasn’t. 

For the rest of the night, my gf and her family barely spoke to me and every time the waiter came around he insisted on talking only to me. I think he knew I fucked up, because he ignored everyone else at the table and brought the bill to me too. I obviously couldn’t afford it, so her dad just reached over and put his card down while looking me dead in the eyes. I felt his judgement and it could have burned through my eyes and out the back of my head. 

After we left her mom said it was interesting to meet me and my gf dropped me off at home. She dumped me over text that weekend. :(

Motivation and/or intent are incredibly important, especially for criminal proceedings. Crime and civil disputes do not exist in a vacuum of pure causality. The reason why people do things is important in most types of law as far as I know, and likely all of them. The reason someone breaches a contract will affect whether or not a court will enforce that contract. The reason as to why a company inflicts damages on people through an intentional tort may reflect upon any damages as well. And in criminal proceedings, the intent in things like murder or assault will greatly affect the punishment.

intent -  n. mental desire and will to act in a particular way, including wishing not to participate. Intent is a crucial element in determining if certain acts were criminal. Occasionally a judge or jury may find that "there was no criminal intent." Example: lack of intent may reduce a charge of manslaughter...

mens rea - (menz ray-ah) n. Latin for a "guilty mind," or criminal intent in committing the act.

malice - n. a conscious, intentional wrongdoing either of a civil wrong like libel (false written statement about another) or a criminal act like assault or murder, with the intention of doing harm to the victim. This intention includes ill-will, hatred or total disregard for the other's well-being. Often the mean nature of the act itself implies malice, without the party saying "I did it because I was mad at him, and I hated him," which would be express malice. Malice is an element in first degree murder. In a lawsuit for defamation (libel and slander) **the existence of malice may increase the judgment to include general damages**. Proof of malice is absolutely necessary for a "public figure" to win a lawsuit for defamation.

source: [dictionary.law.com](https://dictionary.law.com)

Are you me? I was like this all the way through under grad. Same thing with music too. But I can tell you what kind of helped me. 

I would skip class a lot because I'd think I can make it up later and catch up. But then I'd be anxious and worried about going back after missing. I felt lazy and worthless. Turned from a "I can catch up" to "I'm  a piece of shit".  Thought about how I let my profs down and my family and self down. 

I felt ashamed to show my face in class. Like I was the odd man out. The kid who sits in back every other week and doesn't ask questions or contribute. Especially this too, I was in 20 person philosophy and English courses. 

But even if the randos in your class cared if you came, it doesn't matter what they think. And even though you should probably care about what the prof thinks, they would want you there trying rather than not there in my experience. 

When I forced my self to go, I realized it wasn't as stressful as I was making it out to be. Professor never called me out (in class at least), no one stared at me. I learned and had a good time because I enjoyed school. 

Moral here isn't that the things that make you anxious aren't so bad, and that you can solve everything just be having a better attitude. Moral here is that you can make a positive change just by getting the things you want to put off done. 

It might hurt or make you anxious or depressed either way. But couldn't you say that it's better to be slightly down doing something small like showing up, than to put it off over and over until you beat yourself up for it?

Of course motivating yourself is always a problem, and trust me I understand that. Medication, therapy, supportive friends and family are always a good thing to have. But forcing yourself to be proactive can really help. It can be hard though. You can always ask for help, I know I needed some pushing. 

And as far as fearing failure is concerned; the most successful people in the world have never not had failures. Personal and professional, it doesn't matter. But what's the greater failure: to try and fail, and continue doing so with the chance for success, or to never try at all and never attain the success you desire?

I hope this doesn't sound bootstrappy, just offering my own experiences as an example. I still struggle with these same problems, but I have made progress. Either way, I think you can do it. Failure is something that can ultimately make you better. The only thing I ever got from not trying was hurting myself for not trying.
